summary: Lists requirements for performing traffic engineering over MPLS networks. It identifies the capabilities needed to use network resources efficiently and make operations reliable, guiding later protocol work. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Traffic engineering is picking smart routes so roads do not jam. This memo lists what a road system needs to be able to do for that.

questions: what is traffic engineering over mpls
subtitle: What an MPLS network must be able to do so operators can steer traffic around congestion instead of letting shortest paths pile up.

tldr.problem: Shortest-path interior routing protocols ignore bandwidth and load, so traffic streams converge on the same links and cause congestion even when other paths have spare capacity.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists the capabilities MPLS needs for traffic engineering: attributes on traffic trunks, attributes on network resources, and a constraint-based routing framework that picks label switched paths subject to them.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements memo from operators of a large backbone, intended to guide MPLS specifications and implementations. It defines no protocol itself.

facts.label: Trunk operations
facts.value: Establish, activate, deactivate, modify, reroute, destroy

today: RFC 2702 is an Informational memo and its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records requirements as of September 1999 and does not define a protocol.

sections.title: Why Traffic Engineering Is Needed
sections.content:
Traffic engineering (TE) is the measurement, modeling, characterization and control of Internet traffic to reach specific performance objectives. The RFC splits the objectives into traffic oriented ones (less packet loss and delay, more throughput, honoring service level agreements) and resource oriented ones (do not leave some links overloaded while others sit idle). Minimizing prolonged congestion is the main goal of both.

The RFC separates two causes of congestion. Too little capacity can be fixed by adding capacity or by classical congestion control. Congestion from inefficient mapping of traffic onto resources is the part traffic engineering addresses, typically through load balancing.

Existing interior gateway protocols (IGPs) are blamed for part of the problem. They use shortest-path algorithms with a simple additive metric and are topology driven, so bandwidth availability is not considered. Equal-cost load sharing helps with some cases but not in large, dense networks. Operators had worked around this with overlay models such as IP over ATM or frame relay, and the RFC wants MPLS to offer at least the same functionality.
sections.plainLanguage: Normal routing always picks the shortest road, even when it is packed. Traffic engineering means sometimes picking a longer, emptier road so everybody gets there faster.

sections.title: Traffic Trunks and the Induced MPLS Graph
sections.content:
The RFC builds on MPLS, where short fixed-length labels assigned at the ingress to an MPLS domain drive forwarding. Its central object is the traffic trunk: an aggregate of traffic flows of the same class placed inside a label switched path (LSP). A trunk is unidirectional and routable, and it is distinct from the LSP it uses, so it can be moved from one path to another. The RFC admits that in practice the two terms are often used synonymously.

The set of LSRs that are endpoints of LSPs, together with those LSPs as logical point-to-point links, forms the induced MPLS graph, analogous to a virtual topology in an overlay model. The RFC states three problems: mapping packets to forwarding equivalence classes, mapping those classes to traffic trunks, and mapping trunks onto the physical network through LSPs. It focuses only on the third.

Why MPLS suits TE, in the RFC's list: explicit LSPs not tied to destination-based forwarding, efficient maintenance of LSPs, attributes on trunks and on resources, support for both aggregation and disaggregation of traffic, easy integration with constraint-based routing, and potentially lower overhead than the alternatives.
sections.plainLanguage: A traffic trunk is like a bundle of cars of the same kind all travelling together. The bundle can be moved to a different road without changing what it carries.

sections.title: Traffic Trunk Attributes
sections.content:
Section 5 lists attributes that should shape how each trunk behaves, and says it should be possible to change them administratively.

  • Traffic parameters: peak rate, average rate, permissible burst size, from which resource needs are computed.
  • Path selection: an operator-specified explicit path can be mandatory (use only this path, otherwise setup fails, and the path is implicitly pinned) or non-mandatory (use it if feasible). Candidate paths can be ranked, and resource class affinity attributes include or exclude classes of resources.
  • Adaptivity: whether the trunk may be re-optimized onto better paths when the network changes. Frequency of re-optimization should be configurable for stability.
  • Load distribution: parallel trunks between two nodes should be able to carry configured proportions of the traffic, keeping packets of one micro-flow in order.
  • Priority and preemption: priority orders path selection; preemption has four modes (preemptor enabled, non-preemptor, preemptable, non-preemptable) with non-preemptor and non-preemptable as the default.
  • Resilience: what to do when a path fails, from not rerouting to rerouting over any available path.
  • Policing: what to do with a trunk that exceeds its contract: rate limit, tag or forward it. Policing is best done at the network ingress.

A trunk A can preempt B only if A has higher priority, they contend for a resource, the resource cannot hold both, A is preemptor enabled, and B is preemptable.

The basic operations on a trunk are establish, activate, deactivate, modify attributes, reroute and destroy. Statistics at the trunk level are called essential.
sections.plainLanguage: Each bundle of traffic gets a set of instructions: how much it needs, which roads it must use or avoid, who goes first in a squeeze, and what to do if a road closes.

sections.title: Resource Attributes
sections.content:
Resources, mainly links, carry attributes that constrain which trunks may be placed on them. The maximum allocation multiplier sets what proportion of a resource, usually link bandwidth, can be allocated to trunks. A resource is under-allocated if aggregate demands always stay below capacity, and over-allocated if they can exceed it, which exploits the fact that peak demands may not coincide in time.

A resource class works like a color assigned to resources. Trunks can then be steered toward or away from a color, and the RFC gives examples such as applying one policy to scattered resources, restricting trunks to a subset of links, or containing local traffic within a region. A resource can have more than one class; the RFC's example is giving all OC-48 links a distinguished class.
sections.plainLanguage: Roads get colored labels, such as red roads and blue roads. A bundle of traffic can then be told to use only blue roads, or to stay off red ones.

sections.title: Constraint-Based Routing
sections.content:
Section 7 asks for a constraint-based routing framework that lets a demand-driven, resource-aware paradigm coexist with hop-by-hop IGPs. For each trunk starting at a node, it takes the trunk attributes, the resource attributes and other topology state, and computes an explicit route, meaning an LSP that satisfies the demands within the constraints. This cuts manual configuration, though an operator can still configure explicit routes for fine-grained tuning.

The general problem is intractable for most realistic constraints, but a simple heuristic finds a feasible path for a single trunk if one exists: first prune resources that fail the trunk's requirements, then run a shortest path algorithm on what remains. Ties should be broken to minimize congestion. With multiple trunks, the heuristic may fail to find a mapping even when one exists.

The RFC suggests two ways to add this to routers: extend IGPs such as OSPF and IS-IS, or add a constraint-based routing process beside the IGP process, as in its Figure 1. It leaves open how topology state is exchanged and maintained.
sections.plainLanguage: First cross off every road that is too small or off limits. Then pick the shortest road among the ones left.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it introduces no new security issues beyond those inherent in MPLS. It adds one point: changes to the administratively configurable parameters must be made securely, by authorized entities.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the people in charge should be allowed to change the traffic rules, or someone could send everyone down the wrong road.
